L97@P3-4: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 41. Introduction
L98@P4: Glaucoma is a leading
L99@P4: cause of blindness
L100@P4: affecting an estimated
L101@P4: at 80 million people
L102@P4: worldwide. It is an
L103@P4: intermittently progressive
L104@P4: optic neuropathy that
L105@P4: results in visual field
L106@P4: defects with a pattern that
L107@P4: locates the pathological lesion in the pre-laminar
L108@P4: optic nerve head. A reduction in intraocular
L109@P4: pressure will slow or arrest progression of the
L110@P4: disease in the vast majority of cases.
L111@P4: Glaucoma is traditionally divided into primary
L112@P4: and secondary variants. The secondary form is a
L113@P4: result of another ophthalmic or systemic disease
L114@P4: which typically provokes a marked elevation
L115@P4: of intraocular pressure. Common underlying
L116@P4: conditions include neovascularization, uveitis or
L117@P4: ocular trauma.
L118@P4: The primary variant of glaucoma occurs without
L119@P4: evidence of a secondary precipitating disease.
L120@P4: Primary glaucoma is classified according to
L121@P4: the appearance of the iridocorneal angle.
L122@P4: Aqueous humour drains out of the eye mainly
L123@P4: via the trabecular meshwork, in the iridocorneal
L124@P4: angle. Depending on whether the iris is, or
L125@P4: is not, occluding the angle, two variants are
L126@P4: termed primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG)
L127@P4: and primary open angle glaucoma (POAG)
L128@P4: respectively.
L129@P4: POAG and PACG are fundamentally different
L130@P4: in their clinical presentation and in their
L131@P4: management pathways. PACG is a more
L132@P4: pressure dependent disease than open-angle
L133@P4: glaucoma. The treatment of PACG focuses on
L134@P4: decompartmentalising the eye to break down
L135@P4: barriers to circulation of aqueous flow inside the
L136@P4: eye.
L137@P4: The natural history of PACG is typically divided
L138@P4: into three stages. The first stage is termed
L139@P4: suspected primary angle-closure and those
L140@P4: affected are called primary angle-closure
L141@P4: suspects (PACS). In this stage of the condition,
L142@P4: there is contact between the iris and the
L143@P4: trabecular meshwork but the intraocular pressure
L144@P4: (IOP) is normal, there are no acquired adhesions
L145@P4: between the iris and the corneoscleral coat
L146@P4: (peripheral anterior synechiae – PAS). The optic
L147@P4: nerve structure and visual function are normal.
L148@P4: Primary angle-closure (PAC) is the second
L149@P4: stage in which the IOP has become elevated
L150@P4: (either previously or currently), and/or there are
L151@P4: peripheral anterior synechial scars that have
L152@P4: developed between the iris and the trabecular
L153@P4: meshwork. In this stage there is no evidence of
L154@P4: glaucomatous damage to the optic nerve nor any
L155@P4: visual field abnormality.
L156@P4: The third and final stage is the development of
L157@P4: primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG). It is
L158@P4: possible for patients to develop PACG without
L159@P4: elevated IOP having been detected and also in
L160@P4: the absence of PAS.
L161@P4: The florid, symptomatic presentation of angleclosure, called acute angle-closure (AAC),
L162@P4: is the result of sudden, total occlusion of the
L163@P4: trabecular meshwork which causes extreme
L164@P4: ocular hypertension. Symptoms of pain, sudden
L165@P4: reduction (or even loss) of vision, nausea and/
L166@P4: or vomiting can be profound and dramatic.
L167@P4: Previously, AAC was regarded as a “rapidly
L168@P4: blinding” condition. With prompt presentation
L169@P4: and appropriate management, this condition is
L170@P4: not as feared as it once was.
L171@P4: PACG causes a higher rate of severe visual
L172@P4: loss than does POAG. Although POAG affects
L173@P4: approximately three times as many people
L174@P4: globally as does PACG (60 million versus 20
L175@P4: million), the numbers of people blinded by
L176@P4: POAG and PACG are roughly equal. This greater
L177@P4: propensity to cause serious loss of vision makes
L178@P4: clinicians justifiably cautious in managing PACG
L179@P4: and has prompted many to consider preventive
L180@P4: treatment.
L181@P4: 1.1 Background
L182@P4: 80 million
L183@P4: people
L184@P4-5: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 5Angle-closure
L185@P5: glaucoma typically
L186@P5: affects elderly patients.
L187@P5: PACG is
L188@P5: rare among adults
L189@P5: under the age of 40
L190@P5: and, when it does
L191@P5: occur, is thought to
L192@P5: be predominantly the result of a plateau iris
L193@P5: mechanism. The disease is very rare but has
L194@P5: been documented in children.
L195@P5: Angle-closure occurs with approximately
L196@P5: a 3:1 female to male ratio. Racial heritage
L197@P5: is a widely recognised risk factor for angleclosure disease. Asian people suffer a higher
L198@P5: burden of angle-closure, with a three-fold
L199@P5: greater incidence of acute angle-closure in
L200@P5: Chinese patients compared to Caucasians.
L201@P5: Angle-closure glaucoma is uncommon
L202@P5: among Africans.
L203@P5: See aao.org
L204@P5: In September 1857, Albrecht von Graefe
L205@P5: reported the use of surgical iridectomy in the
L206@P5: management of glaucoma. Surgical iridectomy
L207@P5: has since been a cornerstone of management
L208@P5: of angle-closure glaucoma until the mid 1970’s
L209@P5: when it was superseded by laser peripheral
L210@P5: iridotomy (LPI). LPI has been widely used as a
L211@P5: treatment but also increasingly deployed as a
L212@P5: preventative strategy. The role of preventive LPI
L213@P5: in the fellow eye of someone who has suffered
L214@P5: an acute angle-closure crisis is unquestioned.
L215@P5: The publication of the results of the EAGLE
L216@P5: trial in 2016, has provided new evidence to
L217@P5: guide the management of PAC and PACG. This
L218@P5: trial randomised patients with either PAC with
L219@P5: IOP above 30 mmHg, or with PACG, to receive
L220@P5: either LPI or clear lens phacoemulsification.
L221@P5: EAGLE represents probably the most significant
L222@P5: advance in the management of angle-closure
L223@P5: glaucoma since the invention of the surgical
L224@P5: iridectomy. It is now clear that lens extraction
L225@P5: is generally safe, highly effective, cost-effective
L226@P5: and benefits patient’s quality of life compared
L227@P5: to LPI in patients meeting enrolment criteria.
L228@P5: This has led to a profound shift in management
L229@P5: away from the use of LPI in PAC and PACG.
L230@P5: The use of LPI as a preventative treatment
L231@P5: in people who are asymptomatic and have
L232@P5: never had a documented pressure rise is
L233@P5: widely practiced but has no firm evidence

L257@P5-6: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 6base. Around 75% of all UK ophthalmology
L258@P6: consultants offer a prophylactic LPI to patients
L259@P6: with narrow or occluded drainage angles.
L260@P6: The events of the first six months of 2020
L261@P6: have brought the NHS under unprecedented
L262@P6: pressure, and is prompting a fundamental reexamination of the justification for previously
L263@P6: entrenched patterns of practice.
L264@P6: In the year 2018-19, NHS hospital statistics
L265@P6: for England recorded 13,844 patient episodes
L266@P6: with a primary procedure identified as LPI.
L267@P6: The majority of these will have related to
L268@P6: prophylactic procedures. This represents
L269@P6: significant capacity burden and, therefore,
L270@P6: the role of LPI needs to be very carefully
L271@P6: scrutinised.
L272@P6-7: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 72. Objectives
L273@P7: 2.1 Main Aims
L274@P7: The scope of this guideline covers the primary angle-closure spectrum only and specifically excludes
L275@P7: secondary disease such as that resulting from uveitis or neovascularization.
L276@P7: This guideline has been written primarily for clinicians involved in eye care in the community and in
L277@P7: hospital eye services and aims to inform clinicians on 4 main points
L278@P7: 1. What is the accuracy of current diagnostic tests
L279@P7: 2. What is the effectiveness of different interventions
L280@P7: 3. When to refer to hospital eye services
L281@P7: 4. When to discharge to community
L282@P7: 2.2 Key Clinical questions
L283@P7: Epidemiology
L284@P7: a. What is the Primary Angle Closure spectrum of disease and how should patients be classified?
L285@P7: b. What is the prevalence in the UK (or Europe/White US if minimal data exists for the UK)
L286@P7: c. What is the visual morbidity (including notifiable sight impairment) caused by PACG in the
L287@P7: UK (or Europe/White US if there is minimal data for the UK)?
L288@P7: d. What are the known risk factors for PACG?
L289@P7: e. What is the natural history of untreated and treated disease?
L290@P7: Diagnosis
L291@P7: f. What is/are the optimal and/or acceptable test(s) for diagnosis (secondary/tertiary)
L292@P7: g. Should provocative tests be used?
L293@P7: h. What is the optimal and/or acceptable test(s) for case detection (optom/primary care)
L294@P7: Management of primary angle-closure disease?
L295@P7: i. When to do a prophylactic laser iridotomy
L296@P7: j. Laser iridotomy as prophylaxis in the fellow eye of people suffering acute angle-closure
L297@P7: k. What is the optimal and/or acceptable management of an acute angle-closure crisis
L298@P7: l. What is the optimal and/or acceptable management of primary angle-closure with glaucoma
L299@P7: m.What systematic reviews and meta-analyses exist that can guide management?
L300@P7: n. What are the appropriate laser, medical and surgical interventions in established disease?
L301@P7: o. Is there evidence that management should differ in different racial groups (For instance,
L302@P7: should Asian or African people be offered different management)?
L303@P7-8: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 8Patient Follow up
L304@P8: p. How to manage residual iridotrabecular contact (ITC)
L305@P8: q. Management of cataract in angle-closure (whether to perform LPI before phaco?)
L306@P8: r. How to handle pupil dilation in suspected or established angle-closure
L307@P8: 3. Methods
L308@P8: 3.1 Search strategy
L309@P8: Key questions for the guideline were developed using the PICO framework to provide a structured basis
L310@P8: for identifying the evidence. A systematic review of the literature was undertaken using the explicit
L311@P8: search strategies devised in collaboration with the Cochrane Eyes and Vision Group. Databases
L312@P8: searched include Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for literature published between 2000
L313@P8: & 2017. Further searches were undertaken on various websites including the US National Guidelines
L314@P8: Clearinghouse.
L315@P8: The evidence base for this guideline was identified and synthesized in accordance with the accepted
L316@P8: methodology. Each of the selected papers was evaluated by the guideline development group using
L317@P8: standard checklists before conclusions were considered as acceptable evidence. The literature search
L318@P8: focused on the best available evidence to address the key review questions by including the following
L319@P8: types of evidence
L320@P8: • Published guidelines
L321@P8: • Systematic reviews
L322@P8: • Randomised controlled trials
L323@P8: • Cohort and case control studies
L324@P8: • Case series
L325@P8: Papers not published in the English language, conference abstracts and letters were excluded.
L326@P8: 3.2 Evidence and grading
L327@P8: We graded the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in line with the system
L328@P8: published by the GRADE Working Group1
L329@P8: :
L330@P8: Levels of evidence
L331@P8: • High = Further research is very unlikely to change our confidence in the estimate of effect
L332@P8: (e.g., large, well conducted, definite RCTs)
L333@P8: • Moderate = Further research is likely to have an important impact on our confidence in the
L334@P8: estimate of effect and may change the estimate (e.g., small or potentially biased RCTs,
L335@P8: non-randomised comparative studies)
L336@P8: • Low = Further research is very likely to have an important impact on our confidence in the
L337@P8: estimate of effect and is likely to change the estimate (e.g., observational studies)
L338@P8: • Very low = Any estimate of effect is very uncertain.
L339@P8-9: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 94. Recommendation for Practice
L340@P9: • Strong: “Do it” or “don’t do it” – indicating a judgment that most well-informed people would
L341@P9: make;
L342@P9: (e.g., large, well conducted, definite RCTs)
L343@P9: • Weak: “Probably do it” or “probably don’t do it” – indicating a judgment that a majority of well
L344@P9: informed people would make but a substantial minority would not.
L345@P9: 4.1 Terminology & Disease Definitions
L346@P9: Primary angle-closure is defined by contact between the iris and trabecular meshwork in the absence
L347@P9: of other ocular or systemic diseases (e.g. uveitis or neovascularization). Primary irido-trabecular
L348@P9: contact (ITC) is therefore the hallmark of the disease, which may sometimes lead to secondary
L349@P9: elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP). This may in turn cause sight loss as a result of glaucoma, or
L350@P9: sometimes through other diseases such as cataract or retinal vascular disease. Glaucoma denotes
L351@P9: damage to the retinal ganglion cell axons at the level of the pre-laminar optic nerve head causing
L352@P9: reproducible visual field loss. Glaucoma is slowed or arrested by reduction of intraocular pressure.
L353@P9: Primary angle-closure glaucoma, therefore, indicates loss of visual function and structural damage
L354@P9: to the optic nerve occurring in the setting of an occluded drainage angle, with an assumed underlying
L355@P9: mechanism mediated by elevated intraocular pressure. As with all forms of glaucoma, other
L356@P9: explanations for loss of vision should be considered
L357@P9: and if necessary, excluded by further investigation.
L358@P9: The acute presentation of angle-closure is a well-known ophthalmic emergency. This sudden, profound
L359@P9: ocular hypertension causes dramatic symptoms. Both the disease and the ensuing medical treatment
L360@P9: can make patients seriously ill. Acute symptoms are associated with presentation earlier in the natural

L14: # Qu'est-ce qu'un glaucome aigu par fermeture d l'angle ?
L15: Parallèlement au glaucome chronique insidieux et asymptomatique abordé précédemment, il existe un autre type de glaucome, appelé le glaucome aigu. Celui-ci diffère du glaucome chronique à angle ouvert sur de nombreux points : le glaucome aigu à angle fermé survient soudainement et s’accompagne de nombreux symptômes tels que des douleurs, des rougeurs, des maux de tête, voire des vomissements et une perte de vision importante en peu de temps.
L16: La pression s’élève très rapidement (en quelques heures) à des niveaux très élevés (parfois plus de 60 mm Hg), à la suite d’une adhérence de la base de l’iris à la cornée. Le tamis de l’angle est alors complètement obturé (d’où le nom de glaucome aigu à angle fermé) : le drainage de l’humeur aqueuse est totalement bloqué de manière abrupte.
L17: Une telle crise survient souvent en début de soirée ou pendant la nuit.  La douleur intense et le trouble soudain de la vision amènent généralement les personnes atteintes d’un glaucome aigu à être hospitalisées d’urgence. De plus, il est impératif de commencer le traitement rapidement, faute de quoi la perte sévère de la vision sera permanente. Pour ce type de glaucome, il existe des mesures de prévention.
L18: L’ophtalmologue parvient généralement à reconnaître les facteurs anatomiques qui prédisposent une personne à développer une crise de glaucome aigu à angle fermé. Dans ce cas, un simple traitement préventif au laser peut réduire le risque de crise.

L24: Le glaucome aigu est plus répandu chez les femmes ou les patients souffrant d’hypermétropie ou de cataracte avancée (opacification et gonflement du cristallin). Il est également à noter que la prise de certains médicaments peut déclencher une crise de glaucome aigu. Vous trouverez cette information sur la notice de nombreux médicaments, notamment ceux contre le rhume, la diarrhée, la dépression et la maladie de Parkinson.
L25: Dans la plupart des cas, il s’agit de médicaments qui provoquent une dilatation de la pupille et qui peuvent donc induire un glaucome aigu chez les patients prédisposés. Ces médicaments n’ont aucun effet sur le glaucome chronique.
